questions.stem: A 68-year-old kidney transplant recipient hospitalized for pneumonia develops a painful vesicular rash confined to one band across the left trunk that does not cross the midline. Intravenous acyclovir is started. Which of the following best describes how this drug interferes with viral replication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks viral attachment by occupying the host cell surface receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: It competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate for incorporation into viral DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits viral neuraminidase and blocks release of newly formed virions

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and terminates the RNA chain

choices.label: E
choices.text: It inhibits viral thymidine kinase and prevents nucleoside phosphorylation

explanation.summary: Acyclovir is a guanosine analog that is incorporated into growing viral DNA and prevents strand lengthening.
explanation.whyCorrect: Guanosine analogs are guanosine (a purine) attached to a sugar, so their chemical structure mimics nucleosides. The activated triphosphate competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate for incorporation into the growing viral DNA strand, and once added it prevents further lengthening of that strand. The result is reduced viral DNA synthesis and reduced viral proliferation, which shortens the duration and severity of a reactivation such as this dermatomal zoster.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No antiherpetic drug in this class acts at receptor binding or viral entry; they all act at nucleic acid synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neuraminidase inhibition is the mechanism of oseltamivir, an influenza drug, and is not how any antiherpetic agent works.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting RNA-dependent RNA polymerase with chain termination describes sofosbuvir, used for hepatitis C, not acyclovir.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral thymidine kinase is the enzyme that activates acyclovir, not the enzyme acyclovir inhibits.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Acyclovir and the other guanosine analogs have very little activity in uninfected human cells. Which of the following best explains this specificity for herpesviruses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human cells do not use the guanosine nucleotides that these drugs resemble

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are actively transported only into cells displaying viral surface antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are destroyed by human enzymes before they can reach the cell nucleus

choices.label: D
choices.text: They bind irreversibly to the viral capsid before the particle enters a cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: They must be phosphorylated by virus-specific kinases present in infected cells

explanation.summary: Guanosine analogs are specific for herpesviruses because viral kinases are required to activate them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir, and ganciclovir are prodrug-like nucleoside analogs that must be phosphorylated before they can be incorporated into DNA. That first phosphorylation is carried out by virus-specific enzymes such as thymidine kinase and UL97, which are present only where the virus is replicating. Drug is therefore activated preferentially inside infected cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Human cells use guanosine nucleotides constantly; that is precisely why these drugs are not perfectly selective.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Selectivity comes from intracellular activation, not from a transport system that recognizes viral antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The drugs are active in infected human cells, so host degradation cannot be the basis of their selectivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These agents act on DNA synthesis inside the cell and have no effect on the capsid of an extracellular virion.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with AIDS has perianal herpes simplex ulcers that continue to enlarge despite several weeks of oral acyclovir followed by valacyclovir. A viral isolate is confirmed to be drug resistant. Which of the following changes in the virus is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mutation in the host DNA polymerase gene that reduces drug binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mutation in the UL97 phosphotransferase gene carried by the virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: A mutation that results in decreased viral thymidine kinase activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overproduction of viral DNA polymerase that outcompetes the drug

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of an efflux pump that exports drug from the infected cell

explanation.summary: Acyclovir resistance in herpes simplex is caused by mutations that lower viral thymidine kinase activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thymidine kinase phosphorylation is the first step in activating acyclovir and its relatives. A mutation that decreases thymidine kinase activity decreases the amount of active drug generated inside the infected cell, so the drug fails despite adequate dosing. Resistant herpesvirus strains are found primarily in immunosuppressed patients such as this one, where a persistently high viral load and chronic antiviral exposure give resistant strains the chance to emerge.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Resistance is a property of the virus; a host polymerase mutation is not a described mechanism of antiherpetic failure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: UL97 mutation is the resistance mechanism for ganciclovir in cytomegalovirus, not for acyclovir in herpes simplex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resistance arises from failure to activate the drug, not from making more of the polymerase target.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Efflux pump upregulation is not a described mechanism of herpesvirus resistance to these agents.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: The patient described above has herpes simplex ulcers caused by a strain with markedly reduced thymidine kinase activity. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate choice for his infection?

explanation.summary: Foscarnet is the drug of choice for thymidine kinase-deficient, acyclovir-resistant herpes simplex.
explanation.whyCorrect: Foscarnet inhibits the viral DNA polymerase directly and does not need to be activated by a viral enzyme first. Because the resistance mechanism here is loss of the activating kinase, foscarnet bypasses the problem entirely and remains effective.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acyclovir is the drug that already failed; the thymidine kinase mutation is specifically resistance to it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Famciclovir is in the same family and shares the same activation step, so the mutation confers resistance to it as well.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penciclovir also requires viral kinase activation and is only a topical agent for orolabial herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Valacyclovir is a prodrug of acyclovir and still depends on viral thymidine kinase for activation.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with AIDS is treated with foscarnet for a herpesvirus infection. Which of the following best characterizes this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A guanosine analog that terminates the chain after viral kinase activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A neuraminidase inhibitor that prevents budding of virions from the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: A nucleoside analog phosphorylated by host kinases to an active triphosphate

choices.label: D
choices.text: A protease inhibitor that blocks cleavage of viral polyprotein precursors

choices.label: E
choices.text: A pyrophosphate analog that noncompetitively inhibits viral polymerases

explanation.summary: Foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analog and a noncompetitive inhibitor of viral RNA and DNA polymerases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Foscarnet belongs to the viral DNA polymerase inhibitor class along with cidofovir. It is a pyrophosphate analog rather than a nucleoside analog, and it acts as a noncompetitive inhibitor of many viral RNA and DNA polymerases. Because it does not need phosphorylation by a viral enzyme, it works against strains that have lost their activating kinase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: That describes acyclovir and its relatives, which are nucleoside analogs activated by viral kinases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neuraminidase inhibition is an influenza drug mechanism and has no role against herpesviruses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Host kinase activation describes cidofovir; foscarnet is not a nucleoside analog and is not phosphorylated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No antiherpetic agent covered here acts as a protease inhibitor.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 55-year-old transplant recipient receiving intravenous ganciclovir for cytomegalovirus disease has a leukocyte count of 1,800/mm3, platelet count of 62,000/mm3, and hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL. Which of the following adverse effects of this drug best accounts for these findings?

explanation.summary: Ganciclovir characteristically causes leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the antiherpetic drugs, ganciclovir is the one associated with myelosuppression. The expected pattern is exactly what this patient shows: a low white cell count, a low platelet count, and anemia. Blood counts must therefore be followed during ganciclovir therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ganciclovir is not described as a cause of immune-mediated red cell destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antiherpetic drugs are nucleoside and pyrophosphate analogs, not folate antagonists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired iron absorption would not explain the simultaneous drop in white cells and platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration is not a listed adverse effect of any antiherpetic agent.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with AIDS begins foscarnet therapy. Two days later he reports perioral tingling and develops carpopedal spasm during blood pressure measurement. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is most likely present?

explanation.summary: Foscarnet causes renal impairment together with electrolyte disturbances, notably hypocalcemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond renal impairment, foscarnet is specifically associated with electrolyte derangements including hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and hypomagnesemia. Perioral paresthesias and carpopedal spasm are the classic bedside signs of a low ionized calcium, so electrolytes should be checked and repleted during therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high calcium level would not cause tetany; foscarnet lowers calcium rather than raising it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Foscarnet drives potassium down rather than up, so hypokalemia is the expected direction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium excess is not among the electrolyte disturbances attributed to foscarnet.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphate elevation is not a described foscarnet effect and would not produce these symptoms.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with severe disseminated herpes simplex infection is given high-dose intravenous acyclovir. Over the next 48 hours her serum creatinine rises from 0.8 mg/dL to 2.3 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains this change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct toxic injury to the renal artery endothelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug-induced diuresis producing severe volume depletion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune complex glomerulonephritis triggered by the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of both ureters by retroperitoneal fibrosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Precipitation of crystallized drug within the renal tubules

explanation.summary: Renal impairment from intravenous acyclovir and ganciclovir results from crystal nephropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intravenous acyclovir and ganciclovir can crystallize and precipitate within the renal tubules, a process called crystal nephropathy, which produces an acute rise in creatinine. This is why proper hydration is maintained whenever these agents are given intravenously.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Renal arterial endothelial toxicity is not a described mechanism for these agents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The injury comes from drug precipitating in the tubules, not from excessive urine output.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An immune complex mechanism is not how antiherpetic drugs injure the kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These drugs do not cause retroperitoneal fibrosis or mechanical ureteral obstruction.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman admitted for intravenous acyclovir has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on hospital day 2, and there is erythema and tenderness along the vein used for infusion. Apart from renal impairment, which of the following additional findings fits this drug's adverse effect profile?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Optic neuritis with loss of color vision

explanation.summary: Acyclovir is associated with increased liver enzymes, increased seizure risk, and phlebitis when given intravenously.
explanation.whyCorrect: The adverse effect list specific to acyclovir includes rising liver enzymes and an increased risk of seizures, plus vein irritation when the drug is infused. This patient shows the neurologic and local vascular effects, so an increase in aminotransferases is the expected accompanying laboratory abnormality.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hearing loss is not a described toxicity of acyclovir or any other agent in this group.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Optic neuritis is not among the adverse effects attributed to antiherpetic drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia belong to ganciclovir, not acyclovir.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Electrolyte disturbances of this kind are characteristic of foscarnet.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with frequent recurrences of genital herpes is prescribed valacyclovir instead of acyclovir and asks why. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acts on a different viral enzyme than acyclovir does

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can be applied topically as well as taken by mouth

choices.label: C
choices.text: It does not require activation by any viral kinase enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: It eliminates virus that lies dormant in the sensory neurons

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a prodrug of acyclovir with greater oral bioavailability

explanation.summary: Valacyclovir is a prodrug of acyclovir with better gastrointestinal absorption and bioavailability.
explanation.whyCorrect: A prodrug is metabolized into its active form within the host. Valacyclovir is converted to acyclovir after absorption, and it is absorbed from the gut better than acyclovir itself, so more active drug reaches the circulation from an oral dose. That pharmacokinetic advantage is the reason it is often chosen for oral therapy of recurrent outbreaks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Once converted, valacyclovir is acyclovir and acts by exactly the same mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Valacyclovir is an oral agent; penciclovir is the topical drug in this group.
whyWrongByChoice.C: As an acyclovir prodrug it still depends on viral kinase activation after conversion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No antiherpetic drug clears latent virus from neurons; these agents manage outbreaks but do not cure the infection.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A clinician is choosing among oral agents for an outbreak of orolabial herpes. Famciclovir differs from acyclovir chiefly in which of the following ways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It inhibits viral DNA polymerase without needing activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a prodrug with better gastrointestinal absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a pyrophosphate analog rather than a nucleoside analog

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is available only as an intravenous preparation

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is effective against cytomegalovirus but not against HSV-2

explanation.summary: Famciclovir is a prodrug whose advantage over acyclovir is better gastrointestinal absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Famciclovir and valacyclovir are the two prodrugs among the antiherpetic guanosine analogs, meaning they are metabolized into their active form within the host. Famciclovir's stated advantage is improved gastrointestinal absorption, which makes oral dosing more reliable than with acyclovir.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activation-independent polymerase inhibition describes foscarnet, not famciclovir.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Famciclovir is a guanosine analog; foscarnet is the pyrophosphate analog.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Famciclovir is an oral drug; acyclovir is the only agent in this class given both orally and intravenously.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Famciclovir is used for HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella-zoster virus, not for cytomegalovirus.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has recurrent mild cold sores on the vermilion border of the lip and prefers a cream to pills. Which of the following agents is used topically for this indication?

explanation.summary: Penciclovir is the topical antiherpetic agent, and its use is limited to orolabial herpes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Localized herpes infection can be treated topically or orally, with topical therapy reserved for mild cases because it is less effective than oral therapy. Penciclovir is specifically the topical treatment for orolabial herpes only, which matches this patient's mild recurrent cold sores.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cidofovir is a parenteral drug used mainly for cytomegalovirus retinitis in patients with AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Foscarnet is given intravenously for herpesvirus infection in immunocompromised patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ganciclovir is an intravenous agent used for cytomegalovirus, not a topical cold sore treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Valganciclovir is the oral prodrug of ganciclovir and is used for cytomegalovirus.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Among the guanosine analogs used to treat herpes simplex infection, which drug can be administered both orally and intravenously?

explanation.summary: Acyclovir is the only drug of its class that can be given both by mouth and intravenously.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oral medication is used for primary infection and recurrent outbreaks of oral and genital herpes, while intravenous therapy is reserved for the most severe cases. Acyclovir is the single agent in this class available by both routes, which is why it is the drug reached for in severe or disseminated disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Famciclovir is an oral prodrug and is not given intravenously.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penciclovir is a topical treatment limited to orolabial herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Valacyclovir is an oral prodrug of acyclovir with no intravenous formulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Valganciclovir is given orally; it is the oral counterpart of intravenous ganciclovir.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student has 5 days of fever, sore throat, chills, and fatigue. Examination shows pharyngeal erythema and mild left upper quadrant tenderness, and testing confirms acute Epstein-Barr virus infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

explanation.summary: Infectious mononucleosis is managed symptomatically because antivirals do not alter the illness.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antiviral medications have not been shown to be clinically effective against either the symptoms or the duration of Epstein-Barr virus infection. Management is therefore symptomatic, using acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for fever, sore throat, and malaise.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Foscarnet is reserved for resistant herpesvirus infections in immunocompromised patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ganciclovir is directed at cytomegalovirus and acyclovir-resistant herpes simplex, not mononucleosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acyclovir treats HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella-zoster virus and has no established benefit in Epstein-Barr virus infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Valacyclovir shares acyclovir's spectrum and likewise does not change the course of this illness.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old man has 2 weeks of fever, malaise, and mild lymphadenopathy. Heterophile antibody testing is negative and cytomegalovirus IgM is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

explanation.summary: Cytomegalovirus infection in an immunocompetent host is self-limited and does not require antiviral therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary cytomegalovirus infection in an immunocompetent host ranges from asymptomatic to a mononucleosis-like illness, and when symptomatic it is self-limited and resolves within weeks. Antiviral therapy has not proven effective in these patients because of the high rate of self-resolution, so treatment focuses on symptomatic relief.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cidofovir is used for cytomegalovirus retinitis in patients with AIDS, not in healthy adults.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Foscarnet is used for cytomegalovirus retinitis and resistant infection in immunocompromised hosts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ganciclovir carries myelosuppressive and renal toxicity that is not justified in a self-limited illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Valganciclovir is reserved for immunocompromised patients who are symptomatic or need prophylaxis.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is being discharged after renal transplantation and is to receive oral antiviral prophylaxis against cytomegalovirus. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?

explanation.summary: Valganciclovir is the oral prodrug of ganciclovir and is used for cytomegalovirus in at-risk patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: In immunocompromised patients, antiviral treatment for cytomegalovirus is given when they are symptomatic or as prophylaxis when the risk of complications is increased, as in transplant recipients. Among the cytomegalovirus drugs, valganciclovir is the one given orally, which suits an outpatient prophylaxis regimen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cidofovir is an intravenous drug used primarily for cytomegalovirus retinitis in AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Foscarnet is an intravenous agent used mainly for retinitis and resistant infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ganciclovir is administered intravenously and is not suitable as an oral discharge regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Valacyclovir covers HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella-zoster virus rather than cytomegalovirus.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with AIDS and a CD4 count of 30/mm3 reports floaters and progressive vision loss, and funduscopy shows cytomegalovirus retinitis. Which of the following agents is used specifically for this condition in patients with HIV/AIDS?

explanation.summary: Cidofovir and foscarnet are the viral DNA polymerase inhibitors used for cytomegalovirus retinitis in AIDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cidofovir and foscarnet are the two viral DNA polymerase inhibitors, and both are used primarily in immunocompromised patients. Cidofovir in particular is used for cytomegalovirus retinitis in patients with AIDS, and it is also used off-label for acyclovir-resistant herpes simplex.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acyclovir is used for HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella-zoster virus, not for cytomegalovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Famciclovir shares acyclovir's spectrum and has no role against cytomegalovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penciclovir is a topical agent for orolabial herpes only.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Valacyclovir is a prodrug of acyclovir and does not cover cytomegalovirus.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with HIV taking a tenofovir-containing regimen is diagnosed with cytomegalovirus infection. Adding which of the following drugs poses the greatest risk of severe renal injury because the two agents compete for excretion in the kidney?

explanation.summary: Ganciclovir and tenofovir compete for renal excretion, raising both drug levels and risking severe renal damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is the classic interaction to recognize in an immunocompromised patient with HIV who needs treatment for cytomegalovirus. Ganciclovir and tenofovir directly compete for excretion in the kidneys, so levels of both rise and severe renal damage can follow. The combination should be avoided.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acyclovir does not treat cytomegalovirus and does not share this specific competition with tenofovir.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Famciclovir also has no activity against cytomegalovirus and no comparable tenofovir interaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Foscarnet can cause significant renal impairment on its own but does not have this drug interaction with tenofovir.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Valacyclovir covers HSV and varicella-zoster virus and has no comparable interaction with tenofovir.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Antiherpetic drugs share a pharmacokinetic property that accounts for most of their clinically important drug interactions. Which of the following is that property?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are almost completely bound to plasma albumin

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are eliminated from the body by the kidneys

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are excreted unchanged into the bile and stool

choices.label: D
choices.text: They strongly induce the hepatic cytochrome P450 system

choices.label: E
choices.text: They undergo extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism

explanation.summary: All antiherpetic medications are renally cleared, so nephrotoxic co-medications and renal dysfunction matter most.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because these drugs are renally cleared, any other medication that can be nephrotoxic must be avoided or used cautiously, and the same caution applies in patients who already have altered renal function. This risk climbs in immunocompromised patients and those with chronic illness, who accumulate many medications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: High protein binding is not the property emphasized for these agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These drugs are cleared renally, not by biliary excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enzyme induction is not the described basis of antiherpetic drug interactions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: First-pass metabolism affects oral bioavailability but is not the source of their interactions.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: An otherwise healthy 5-year-old boy has fever, headache, and a diffuse pustular rash consistent with chickenpox that began 2 days ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

explanation.summary: Chickenpox in a healthy child is self-limiting and most often is not treated with an antiviral.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although both chickenpox and shingles can be treated with oral valacyclovir or acyclovir, chickenpox most often is not treated. The virus is self-limiting, an antiviral would shorten symptoms by only a day or two even if started early, and it exposes the child to adverse effects such as renal impairment. The risk outweighs the benefit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intravenous therapy is reserved for the most severe cases, not uncomplicated chickenpox in a healthy child.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ganciclovir is for cytomegalovirus and acyclovir-resistant herpes simplex, and it carries myelosuppressive toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Valganciclovir is a cytomegalovirus drug and is not used for varicella-zoster virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penciclovir is a topical agent for orolabial herpes only and has no role in varicella.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman has 2 days of a painful vesicular rash limited to a single thoracic dermatome. She is otherwise well and able to take oral medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

explanation.summary: Shingles is reactivated varicella-zoster virus and is treated with oral valacyclovir or acyclovir.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shingles is the recurrent breakout rash that follows primary varicella-zoster infection, and it is most common in the elderly. Because valacyclovir and acyclovir cover varicella-zoster virus, oral therapy with either is appropriate for an immunocompetent patient who can take medication by mouth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cidofovir is used chiefly for cytomegalovirus retinitis in patients with AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Foscarnet is reserved for resistant herpesvirus infection in immunocompromised patients.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Valganciclovir is directed at cytomegalovirus, not varicella-zoster virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical penciclovir is limited to orolabial herpes and cannot treat a dermatomal zoster rash.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Varicella-zoster virus, the agent that causes chickenpox and shingles, is also designated as which of the following human herpesviruses?

explanation.summary: Varicella-zoster virus is human herpesvirus 3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Varicella-zoster virus, designated HHV-3, is responsible for chickenpox as the primary infection and shingles as the later reactivation. Like herpes simplex, it lies dormant in the cell bodies of neurons after primary infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HHV-1 refers to herpes simplex virus 1, the cause of orolabial herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HHV-5 is cytomegalovirus, which is treated with a different set of antiviral agents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-6 is a distinct human herpesvirus and is not the cause of chickenpox or shingles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HHV-8 is a separate human herpesvirus unrelated to varicella and zoster.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Cytomegalovirus is also known as which of the following human herpesviruses?

explanation.summary: Cytomegalovirus is human herpesvirus 5.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytomegalovirus, or HHV-5, is transmitted through close contact, sexual contact, blood, and tissue exposure. It is the herpesvirus for which ganciclovir, valganciclovir, cidofovir, and foscarnet are used, chiefly in immunocompromised patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HHV-2 is herpes simplex virus 2, the usual cause of genital herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HHV-3 is varicella-zoster virus, which causes chickenpox and shingles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-6 is a different human herpesvirus and is not cytomegalovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HHV-7 is a separate human herpesvirus unrelated to cytomegalovirus.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Drug names ending in the suffix -cyclovir or -ciclovir identify members of which of the following antiviral classes?

explanation.summary: The -cyclovir and -ciclovir suffixes mark the guanosine analogs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir, and ganciclovir all carry this suffix and are guanosine analogs, a subgroup of the nucleic acid synthesis inhibitors. Recognizing the suffix immediately tells you the drug is activated by viral kinases and works by being incorporated into growing viral DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Interferon inducers are not among the antiherpetic drug classes described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neuraminidase inhibitors are influenza drugs and do not carry this naming convention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Foscarnet is the pyrophosphate analog, and its name does not carry this suffix.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No antiherpetic agent in this brick is a protease inhibitor.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Guanosine analogs mimic nucleosides and become incorporated into growing DNA strands. Which of the following best explains why these drugs nonetheless produce adverse effects in the host?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They accumulate in the brain and displace GABA from receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are converted by hepatic enzymes to a toxic metabolite

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are not specific to viral DNA and also affect mitochondrial DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: They chelate divalent cations needed by host cell enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: They irreversibly inhibit host ribosomal protein synthesis

explanation.summary: Guanosine analogs are not fully specific to viral DNA and also affect mitochondrial DNA, producing side effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viral kinase activation concentrates these drugs in infected cells, but the incorporation step itself is not restricted to viral DNA. Because they also affect mitochondrial DNA in host cells, the class carries a predictable side effect burden despite its relative selectivity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acyclovir increases seizure risk, but displacement of GABA is not the mechanism given.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A hepatic toxic metabolite is not the described basis for their adverse effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cation chelation is not a property of guanosine analogs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These drugs act on nucleic acid synthesis, not on ribosomes or protein translation.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Cidofovir and foscarnet are said to have only quasi-selective toxicity. Which of the following is the basis for that description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The drugs are cleared by the liver so quickly that host tissue exposure stays minimal

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drugs are concentrated inside infected cells by a virus-encoded membrane transporter

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drugs bind the host polymerase reversibly but the viral polymerase covalently

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drugs remain inactive until they are cleaved by a virus-encoded protease enzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: The viral polymerase differs structurally from the human enzyme, which is still partly inhibited

explanation.summary: Viral DNA polymerase differs structurally from the human enzyme, but the selectivity that provides is incomplete.
explanation.whyCorrect: This class acts on viral DNA polymerase by imitating nucleotides. Structural differences between viral and human DNA polymerase allow preferential inhibition of the viral enzyme, but the selectivity is not complete, so some interference with human DNA polymerase remains. That residual host effect is what the term quasi-selective conveys and it underlies the toxicity of these agents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These drugs are renally cleared, and rapid hepatic clearance is not the explanation for selectivity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No viral transporter concentrates these drugs; their selectivity comes from enzyme structure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Differential covalent versus reversible binding is not the described basis of their selectivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protease-dependent activation is not a feature of cidofovir or foscarnet.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: In which of the following patients is a herpesvirus strain resistant to antiviral therapy most likely to emerge?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 70-year-old treated for one episode of thoracic shingles

choices.label: B
choices.text: A healthy 20-year-old with two cold sore outbreaks each year

choices.label: C
choices.text: A healthy 8-year-old child recovering from chickenpox

choices.label: D
choices.text: A man with AIDS on long-term suppressive therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: A pregnant woman treated once for primary genital herpes

explanation.summary: Resistant herpesvirus strains arise almost exclusively in immunosuppressed patients on chronic antiviral therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Resistant strains are found primarily in immunosuppressed patients such as those with AIDS and transplant recipients, and are rare in immunocompetent hosts. The inability to mount an effective immune response leads to a persistently high viral load, and chronic antiviral use against that large viral population gives ample opportunity for resistant strains to develop.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single zoster episode in an immunocompetent patient involves short-term therapy and a controlled viral load.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An immunocompetent host clears virus effectively, and brief intermittent therapy provides little selection pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chickenpox in a healthy child is self-limited and usually is not even treated with an antiviral.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single treatment course in an immunocompetent patient is not the setting in which resistance emerges.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A patient whose herpes simplex infection failed acyclovir because of a thymidine kinase mutation is switched to valacyclovir, with no improvement. Which of the following best explains this second failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Valacyclovir cannot reach therapeutic blood levels when given by mouth

choices.label: B
choices.text: Valacyclovir is a pyrophosphate analog acting at a different target

choices.label: C
choices.text: Valacyclovir is active only against varicella-zoster virus, not herpes simplex

choices.label: D
choices.text: Valacyclovir is inactivated by extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Valacyclovir requires the same viral enzyme for its activation step

explanation.summary: A thymidine kinase mutation confers cross-resistance to every drug in the acyclovir family.
explanation.whyCorrect: All the drugs in the acyclovir family share the same mechanism of action, including the requirement that viral thymidine kinase perform the first phosphorylation. Because the mutation removes that activating step, resistance extends to all of these drugs rather than to acyclovir alone, so switching within the family does not help.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Valacyclovir has better oral bioavailability than acyclovir, so inadequate absorption is not the issue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Foscarnet is the pyrophosphate analog; valacyclovir is a guanosine analog prodrug.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Valacyclovir covers HSV-1 and HSV-2 in addition to varicella-zoster virus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Valacyclovir is a prodrug with better gastrointestinal absorption, so first-pass inactivation is not the problem.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Ganciclovir is used chiefly for cytomegalovirus infection. It is also specifically indicated for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic hepatitis C infection in a transplant recipient

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpes simplex infection that is resistant to acyclovir

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mild orolabial herpes treated topically in a healthy adult

choices.label: E
choices.text: Primary varicella infection in an immunocompetent child

explanation.summary: Ganciclovir is used for cytomegalovirus and for acyclovir-resistant herpes simplex.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the guanosine analogs, acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir are used for HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella-zoster virus, while ganciclovir is set apart for cytomegalovirus and for herpes simplex that has become resistant to acyclovir.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatitis C is treated with direct-acting antivirals, not with an antiherpetic guanosine analog.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antivirals are not clinically effective against the symptoms or duration of Epstein-Barr virus infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penciclovir is the topical agent for orolabial herpes; ganciclovir has no topical role here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chickenpox in a healthy child is self-limited and most often goes untreated.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with AIDS is about to begin foscarnet for a cytomegalovirus infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate step to limit the drug's most common toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer each dose as a rapid intravenous push

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alkalinize the urine with sodium bicarbonate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Give a loop diuretic before each drug infusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Give aggressive prehydration and monitor renal function

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restrict oral fluids for 24 hours before dosing

explanation.summary: Some degree of renal impairment occurs in most patients on foscarnet, and it is managed with prehydration and monitoring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Renal impairment is the adverse reaction shared by all antiherpetic drugs, and foscarnet is the agent in which it occurs in most patients. Renal function must therefore be monitored during use, and the risk is reduced by aggressive prehydration with fluids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A faster infusion does nothing to protect the kidney and would raise peak drug exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Urinary alkalinization is not part of the described strategy for these agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diuresis before dosing would deplete volume and worsen the renal risk rather than reduce it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Withholding fluids is the opposite of what is needed; hydration is protective.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: After the primary infection resolves, herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus persist in the host and may reactivate later when immunity wanes. In which of the following sites do these viruses lie dormant?

explanation.summary: Herpes simplex and varicella-zoster viruses lie dormant in the cell bodies of neurons.
explanation.whyCorrect: After primary infection, both HSV and varicella-zoster virus become latent in neuronal cell bodies and may reactivate in the future when immunity wanes. That latency is why antiherpetic drugs manage outbreaks but cannot cure the infection, and why reactivation such as shingles is more common in elderly and immunosuppressed patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone marrow is where ganciclovir exerts toxicity, not where these viruses remain dormant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Latency in CD4+ T cells is a feature of HIV, not of the herpesviruses described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymph node germinal centers are not the described reservoir for these viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal tubular cells are the site of drug crystal nephropathy, not of viral latency.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has 1 day of burning pain with urination that also persists between voids, worse on one side, with malaise and a low-grade fever. Examination shows multiple ulcerative lesions on an erythematous base around the genital area. Confirmatory testing is sent. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to start now?

explanation.summary: Primary genital herpes from HSV-2 is treated with an oral antiherpetic agent such as acyclovir.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ulcerative lesions on an erythematous base in the genital area with dysuria and systemic symptoms are characteristic of genital herpes caused by HSV-2. Oral medication is used for primary infection and recurrent outbreaks of oral and genital herpes, so acyclovir can be started while confirmatory testing is pending.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cidofovir is used mainly for cytomegalovirus retinitis in patients with AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intravenous therapy is reserved for the most severe cases, and ganciclovir targets cytomegalovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Valganciclovir is a cytomegalovirus drug and is not used for genital herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penciclovir is topical therapy for orolabial herpes only and does not cover genital disease.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Cidofovir is used off-label against herpes simplex isolates that no longer respond to acyclovir. Which of the following best explains why it retains activity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds viral thymidine kinase and restores that enzyme's activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is converted to its active form by a viral phosphotransferase

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is excreted so slowly that resistant virus is eventually overwhelmed

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is phosphorylated by host cell kinases rather than by viral enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: It prevents the virus from binding to the host cell surface receptor

explanation.summary: Cidofovir does not depend on viral enzymes for activation, so viral kinase mutations do not confer resistance to it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Resistance to the -cyclovir and -ciclovir drugs arises because those agents depend on virus-specific enzymes such as thymidine kinase and UL97 for activation. Cidofovir is phosphorylated by host kinases instead, so a virus that has lost thymidine kinase activity still cannot escape it. This is the same logic that makes foscarnet useful in resistant disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No antiviral restores the function of a mutated viral enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: If cidofovir needed a viral phosphotransferase it would share the resistance pattern of the acyclovir family.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antiherpetic drugs are renally cleared, and slow excretion is not a mechanism for overcoming resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cidofovir acts at nucleic acid synthesis, not at viral attachment or entry.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 60-year-old transplant recipient with cytomegalovirus viremia fails to improve on ganciclovir, and testing identifies a UL97 gene mutation in the virus. Which of the following has been suggested as management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add foscarnet or increase the ganciclovir dose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stop ganciclovir and observe without further antiviral therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Switch to oral famciclovir at a standard dose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to oral valacyclovir at a standard dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to topical penciclovir applied twice daily

explanation.summary: Ganciclovir resistance in cytomegalovirus reflects UL97 mutation, and suggested options are adding foscarnet or raising the ganciclovir dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: The UL97 phosphotransferase performs the initial phosphorylation that activates ganciclovir, so a UL97 mutation reduces the amount of active drug generated. There is no clear guideline for treating ganciclovir-resistant cytomegalovirus, but the suggested approaches are to add foscarnet to ganciclovir or to increase the ganciclovir dose.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytomegalovirus complications in an immunocompromised transplant recipient can be severe, so observation alone is inappropriate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Famciclovir likewise has no cytomegalovirus activity and would not address this infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Valacyclovir does not cover cytomegalovirus and depends on the same kind of viral activation step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penciclovir is topical therapy for orolabial herpes and has no role in systemic cytomegalovirus infection.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 17-year-old with infectious mononucleosis returns with noisy breathing, muffled voice, and difficulty swallowing. Which of the following complications of this infection is most likely responsible?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Crystal nephropathy caused by the virus itself

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progressive retinitis with loss of vision

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upper airway obstruction from pharyngeal swelling

explanation.summary: Complications of Epstein-Barr virus infection include splenomegaly and upper airway obstruction from pharyngeal swelling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute Epstein-Barr virus infection causes infectious mononucleosis, and its recognized complications are splenomegaly and upper airway obstruction due to pharyngeal swelling. Noisy breathing and difficulty swallowing in a patient with mononucleosis point to that airway complication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pancreatitis is not among the described complications of Epstein-Barr virus infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Demyelinating polyneuropathy is not one of the listed complications of mononucleosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crystal nephropathy is a toxicity of intravenous acyclovir and ganciclovir, not a viral complication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retinitis is a cytomegalovirus complication seen in patients with AIDS.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a recurrent cold sore asks whether an antiviral cream will work as well as taking pills. Which of the following is the best response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Topical therapy eradicates latent virus, so it is preferred

choices.label: B
choices.text: Topical therapy is less effective than oral therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Topical therapy is the only option for this infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topical therapy must be paired with intravenous therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical therapy works better but injures the kidneys

explanation.summary: Topical antiherpetic therapy is reserved for mild cases because it is less effective than oral therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Localized herpes infection can be treated topically or orally. Topical treatment is usually reserved for mild cases precisely because it is less effective than oral treatment, and oral medication is what is used for primary infection and recurrent outbreaks of oral and genital herpes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No antiherpetic drug clears latent virus; these drugs reduce symptoms but do not cure the infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral therapy is available and is in fact the more effective option for recurrent outbreaks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intravenous therapy is reserved for the most severe cases and is not combined with a cream for a cold sore.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical therapy is the less effective option, and renal injury is associated with systemic rather than topical use.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV infection is started on a regimen containing emtricitabine, a cytosine analogue. The drug competes with the individual nucleotides and is incorporated into the nucleotide chain that is being built as viral RNA is copied into DNA. Which of the following best describes how this drug stops viral replication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds gp41 after gp120 engages, preventing viral fusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds integrase, preventing insertion of DNA into the genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: It blocks protease, preventing cleavage into mature viral units

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits hepatic CYP450, raising levels of other antivirals

choices.label: E
choices.text: It terminates the growing DNA strand, halting reverse transcription

explanation.summary: Nucleotide/nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors are chain terminators that stop reverse transcriptase.
explanation.whyCorrect: NRTIs are analogues of adenosine (tenofovir), cytosine (emtricitabine, lamivudine), guanosine (abacavir), or thymidine (zidovudine). They compete with the natural nucleotides and are incorporated into the growing nucleotide chain, where they act as chain terminators and stop reverse transcriptase. Because retroviruses must convert RNA to DNA to replicate, this blockade halts the viral life cycle, which is why NRTIs are a mainstay of treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding gp41 once it is exposed by gp120 attachment is the mechanism of the fusion inhibitor enfuvirtide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking integrase is the mechanism of the integrase strand transfer inhibitors, not of a nucleoside analogue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking protease is how protease inhibitors stop budding of mature virions, a later step entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting hepatic CYP450 describes the pharmacokinetic enhancers ritonavir and cobicistat.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with HIV infection has efavirenz added to his regimen. Unlike the nucleoside analogues he is already taking, this drug is not incorporated into the elongating DNA strand; instead it attaches directly to a viral enzyme and inactivates it, so that the DNA strand being made is left incomplete and useless. Which enzyme is inactivated?

explanation.summary: NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcriptase by binding directly to the enzyme rather than by chain termination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, like NRTIs, inhibit reverse transcriptase, but they do so by binding directly to the enzyme and inactivating it. This stops the DNA chain from polymerizing and leaves the elongating strand incomplete. NNRTIs such as efavirenz are often used together with NRTIs, especially tenofovir.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatic cytochrome P450 is a host enzyme targeted by boosters, not the viral enzyme inactivated here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Human DNA polymerase is a host enzyme whose inhibition explains NRTI mitochondrial toxicity, not the antiviral effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Integrase is the target of the integrase strand transfer inhibitors such as raltegravir and dolutegravir.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protease is the target of the protease inhibitors, which act at the final budding step.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with drug-resistant HIV infection is started on maraviroc. The drug prevents the virus from binding to a molecule on the surface of the host cell, so that the virus is unable to enter. Which of the following does this drug block?

explanation.summary: Maraviroc is an entry inhibitor that blocks the host CCR5 coreceptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: For HIV to enter a host cell it must first bind a surface receptor and then fuse with the membrane. One of these receptors is CCR5. Maraviroc blocks CCR5, which prevents binding of the virus and leaves it unable to enter the cell. It is sometimes useful in patients with drug-resistant virus infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: gp120 is the viral envelope protein that attaches to the cell; maraviroc acts on the host coreceptor instead.
whyWrongByChoice.C: gp41 is the viral protein bound by enfuvirtide, which blocks fusion rather than receptor binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Integrase is the enzyme that inserts viral DNA into the host genome and is targeted by INSTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protease is an intracellular viral enzyme targeted by protease inhibitors, not by entry inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman with HIV infection is given enfuvirtide. The target of this drug is not accessible on free virions; it becomes exposed only after the virus has bound gp120 to the cell surface, and blocking it prevents the virus from fusing with the membrane and entering the cell. Which of the following is the target?

explanation.summary: Enfuvirtide binds gp41, which is exposed once HIV binds through gp120, and blocks fusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Entry requires binding followed by fusion. Enfuvirtide binds gp41, a viral protein that becomes exposed once HIV binds gp120 to the cell surface. Binding gp41 blocks fusion of the virus with the membrane and therefore blocks its entry into the cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Integrase acts inside the cell after reverse transcription and is targeted by INSTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reverse transcriptase acts after entry and is targeted by NRTIs and NNRTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The CCR5 coreceptor is blocked by maraviroc, which prevents binding rather than fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: p17 is a structural matrix protein of the virion and is not the target of any antiretroviral class here.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with HIV infection is started on raltegravir. Which of the following steps of the retroviral life cycle does this drug block?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of the virus to the CCR5 coreceptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Budding of assembled virions from the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cleavage of polyproteins into mature units

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversion of viral RNA into viral DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insertion of viral DNA into the host genome

explanation.summary: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors block integration of newly made viral DNA into the host cell genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally, newly made viral DNA must be integrated into the host cell's genome, a step catalyzed by the enzyme integrase. Integrase strand transfer inhibitors such as raltegravir inhibit integrase and prevent this DNA from infecting cells. INSTIs are very common components of modern HIV regimens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding to CCR5 is blocked by maraviroc, an entry inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Budding is the final step blocked indirectly by protease inhibitors, not by integrase inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cleavage of polyproteins into mature viral units is blocked by protease inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conversion of RNA into DNA is blocked by NRTIs and NNRTIs acting on reverse transcriptase.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with HIV infection is started on darunavir. Which of the following best describes the effect of this drug on the virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Polyprotein chains are not cut into mature viral proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: The elongating nucleotide chain is terminated prematurely

choices.label: C
choices.text: The virus cannot bind the CCR5 receptor on the cell surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Viral DNA is not inserted into the host cell's own genome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral RNA is not converted into double-stranded viral DNA

explanation.summary: Protease inhibitors block the enzyme that cuts polyproteins into mature viral proteins, preventing formation of mature virions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protease inhibitors act on the final step of replication, which involves budding of the virus from the host cell. Protease is the enzyme responsible for cutting polyprotein chains into the smaller proteins that make up mature HIV units. Inhibiting protease stops mature viral particles from forming, and these drugs are often considered when a patient is not responding to initial antiretroviral therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Premature chain termination describes the nucleoside analogues, which act at reverse transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking CCR5 binding describes maraviroc, an entry inhibitor acting before the virus gets inside.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking insertion of viral DNA into the genome describes the integrase strand transfer inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocking conversion of RNA to DNA describes inhibition of reverse transcriptase by NRTIs and NNRTIs.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with HIV infection is prescribed atazanavir together with low-dose ritonavir. His clinician explains that the second drug is included specifically to raise the concentration of the first. Which of the following best explains this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes are induced

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatic cytochrome P450 metabolism is inhibited

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intestinal absorption of the first drug is increased

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal tubular secretion of the first drug is blocked

choices.label: E
choices.text: The first drug is displaced from plasma proteins

explanation.summary: Ritonavir and cobicistat are pharmacokinetic enhancers that inhibit hepatic CYP450 to raise levels of the boosted drug.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protease inhibitors often require a booster with ritonavir, which is itself a protease inhibitor, or with cobicistat. These boosters inhibit hepatic cytochrome P450, increasing the concentration of the protease inhibitor. This lets the drug be given less frequently, improving adherence, and it also limits the adverse effects seen at higher doses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Induction of CYP450 would lower rather than raise the level of the boosted drug; efavirenz is the inducer discussed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enhanced intestinal absorption is not the described mechanism of ritonavir or cobicistat.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes boosting to CYP450 inhibition, not to blockade of renal elimination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Displacement from plasma proteins is not how these pharmacokinetic enhancers work.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A clinician wants to build an antiretroviral regimen that does not require a pharmacokinetic booster, because the patient is already taking several medications metabolized by cytochrome P450. Which of the following antiretrovirals is most likely to require such a booster and should therefore be avoided?

explanation.summary: Among the integrase inhibitors, elvitegravir is the one that commonly requires boosting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Only a handful of HIV medications require a pharmacokinetic enhancer. The most common ones that need boosters are the protease inhibitors atazanavir, darunavir, and lopinavir, and the integrase strand transfer inhibitor elvitegravir. Avoiding elvitegravir avoids the added CYP450 inhibition from ritonavir or cobicistat.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bictegravir is cleared by CYP450 but is not listed among the drugs that require boosting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dolutegravir is an integrase inhibitor that is not listed as requiring a booster.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Raltegravir is an integrase inhibitor but is not among the drugs listed as requiring a booster.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tenofovir is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor and is not a boosted agent.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman taking a boosted protease inhibitor asks why an extra pill that has no direct antiviral benefit for her was added. Apart from raising the drug concentration, which of the following is the main clinical advantage of adding this agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It broadens the regimen's activity against resistant strains

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can be substituted for one of the two required NRTIs

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lowers the dosing frequency and improves adherence

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: It removes the need for HLA-B*5701 genetic testing

explanation.summary: Boosting prolongs the duration of the drug so it can be taken less often, which improves adherence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ritonavir and cobicistat inhibit CYP enzymes, which prolongs the duration of the boosted drug and decreases how often the patient must take it. Less frequent dosing helps with adherence to the medication. Boosting also limits the adverse effects that would be seen if higher doses were used instead.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Boosters improve pharmacokinetics; they are not described as broadening activity against resistant virus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Boosters do not replace an NRTI; regimens still generally contain two NRTIs plus a third active drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reducing perinatal transmission comes from effective combination therapy during pregnancy, not from the booster itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA-B*5701 testing is required in all HIV-positive patients regardless of the regimen chosen.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 29-year-old treatment-naive woman is newly diagnosed with HIV infection and is ready to begin antiretroviral therapy. Which of the following combinations is most commonly used to initiate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One nucleoside inhibitor plus one fusion inhibitor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two non-nucleoside inhibitors plus one protease inhibitor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two nucleoside inhibitors plus one integrase inhibitor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two protease inhibitors plus one non-nucleoside inhibitor

explanation.summary: Initial HIV therapy is generally two NRTIs plus a third drug from another class, most commonly an INSTI.
explanation.whyCorrect: A multidrug treatment plan best suppresses HIV RNA, and many studies support initiating therapy with two NRTIs plus one drug from another class, most commonly an integrase strand transfer inhibitor. In some cases the third drug may instead be a protease inhibitor or an NNRTI. This multidrug approach reduces morbidity and mortality related to the infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fusion and entry inhibitors are not typically first-line choices.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Three NRTIs is not the described initial approach; the third drug comes from a different class.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Regimens are built on two NRTIs, not on two NNRTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two protease inhibitors is not a standard backbone; only a booster dose of ritonavir accompanies another PI.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with HIV infection has been adherent to a three-drug regimen for two years. Which of the following best describes what this therapy is expected to accomplish?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete eradication of provirus from the host genome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Correction of the proofreading defect of reverse transcriptase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cure of the infection once the viral load is undetectable

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prevention of all resistance mutations for the patient's life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of HIV RNA that slows progression to AIDS

explanation.summary: Combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses HIV RNA and can slow or halt progression to AIDS, but it does not cure the infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Combination therapy is the mainstay of highly active antiretroviral treatment and can slow or halt progression to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. By suppressing viral RNA and reducing the inflammatory immune response, it keeps the CD4 count up. HIV remains incurable, which is why prevention is emphasized so heavily.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Integration of viral DNA into the host genome is one of the reasons HIV cannot be eradicated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lack of proofreading by reverse transcriptase is an intrinsic viral property that drugs do not repair.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An undetectable viral load reflects suppression, not cure; the virus is described as incurable but manageable.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Combination therapy raises the number of mutations needed for resistance but does not prevent all of them.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A student asks why a patient with HIV infection is never treated with a single antiretroviral agent. Which of the following provides the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single agent cannot penetrate the central nervous system

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single agent is always more nephrotoxic than a combination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antiretrovirals are inactive unless a booster is also given

choices.label: D
choices.text: Combination tablets are less expensive than single agents

choices.label: E
choices.text: More mutations are needed for resistance with several drugs

explanation.summary: Multiple drugs are used simultaneously so that the virus must acquire more mutations before it becomes resistant.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV has a high mutation rate because reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading, which lets the virus quickly adapt to treatment. Using several drugs at once increases the number of mutations the virus would need to escape therapy. These medications are therefore always used in combination, which helps reduce resistance rates.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Central nervous system penetration is not the reason given for combination therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nephrotoxicity is drug specific, such as with tenofovir DF or atazanavir, and is not a reason to combine drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only a handful of antiretrovirals require a booster; most are fully active without one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Combination tablets are used to reduce pill burden and improve adherence, not because of cost.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with HIV infection asks why his virus cannot be cured. His physician explains that one property of the viral enzyme that copies RNA into DNA allows the virus to adapt very quickly to treatment. Which of the following is that property?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cuts polyprotein chains into mature viral proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inserts the viral DNA into the host cell's genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is encoded by the host genome rather than by the virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is inhibited by human DNA polymerases during replication

choices.label: E
choices.text: It lacks proofreading, so mutations accumulate rapidly

explanation.summary: Reverse transcriptase does not proofread, so HIV mutates and adapts rapidly.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV is difficult to cure because of two key steps in its replication pathway: the lack of proofreading by reverse transcriptase, which leads to rapid mutation and adaptation, and the incorporation of viral DNA into the host genome. The high mutation rate lets HIV quickly adapt to treatments, which is why multiple drugs must be used at once.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cutting polyproteins into mature viral proteins is the job of protease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inserting viral DNA into the host genome is the job of integrase, and it is the other reason HIV is hard to cure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reverse transcriptase is a viral enzyme, which is precisely why it can be targeted selectively.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Human DNA polymerases are inhibited by NRTIs as an off-target toxicity; they do not inhibit reverse transcriptase.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A physician practicing in the United States is selecting a third agent for a patient with HIV infection and is concerned about pre-existing drug resistance. Which of the following classes is the one most commonly rendered ineffective by resistance in the United States?

explanation.summary: NNRTIs are the class most commonly ineffective because of resistance in the United States.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the virus is drug resistant, treatment must be more selective. NNRTIs are the most common class in the United States to be ineffective because of resistance. In that situation another type of antiretroviral should be considered in addition to the NRTI backbone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fusion and entry inhibitors are reserved agents, and maraviroc is actually useful in drug-resistant infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: INSTIs are very common components of modern regimens and are the usual third drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NRTIs remain a mainstay of treatment and form the backbone of most regimens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protease inhibitors are often chosen when a patient is not responding to initial therapy.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with HIV infection has been taking two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors plus an integrase strand transfer inhibitor but still has detectable HIV RNA after several months of documented adherence. Which of the following classes is most often considered at this point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A pharmacokinetic enhancer used by itself

explanation.summary: Protease inhibitors are often considered when a patient is not responding to initial antiretroviral therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protease inhibitors block the enzyme that cuts polyprotein chains into mature viral units, stopping mature viral particles from forming. They are often considered when a patient is not responding to initial antiretroviral therapy. In initial regimens the third drug is most commonly an INSTI, with a protease inhibitor or NNRTI as alternatives.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pharmacokinetic enhancer has no useful antiviral effect on its own; it is added to boost another drug.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no non-nucleoside agent in this regimen to duplicate, and NNRTIs are the class most often lost to resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fusion and entry inhibitors are not typically first-line or standard second-step choices.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prevents opportunistic infections and has no effect on HIV replication.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with HIV infection and longstanding depression is taking a regimen that includes dolutegravir. He reports that his mood has worsened and that he now has trouble sleeping. Which of the following best describes the adverse effect profile of this drug's class?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Commonly causes a hypersensitivity reaction tied to an HLA allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Commonly causes insulin resistance, hyperlipidemia, and dyslipidemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Commonly causes mitochondrial toxicity with pancreatitis and neuropathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Commonly causes QT prolongation and central nervous system toxicity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Usually well tolerated, but may aggravate psychiatric illness and cause insomnia

explanation.summary: Integrase inhibitors are usually well tolerated but may worsen psychiatric illness and cause insomnia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Integrase inhibitors do not usually cause adverse effects. The possibilities that do occur include worsening of psychiatric illness such as depression, and they may also cause insomnia. That profile, combined with their potency, is part of why INSTIs are very common in modern HIV regimens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The HLA-linked hypersensitivity reaction belongs to abacavir, an NRTI, through HLA-B*5701.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diabetes, insulin resistance, hyperlipidemia, and dyslipidemia are the characteristic protease inhibitor effects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial toxicity presenting as pancreatitis or neuropathy is an NRTI class effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: QT prolongation with CNS toxicity describes the NNRTI efavirenz.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 40-year-old nurse sustains a needlestick injury from a hollow-bore needle contaminated with blood. The source patient appears clinically to have advanced HIV infection, but his test results are still pending. The puncture wound has been scrubbed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Start a single antiretroviral agent and continue it for one year

choices.label: B
choices.text: Start a three-drug regimen and stop it if the source is uninfected

choices.label: C
choices.text: Start a two-drug pre-exposure prophylaxis regimen indefinitely

choices.label: E
choices.text: Withhold antiretrovirals until the source patient's results return

explanation.summary: Occupational postexposure prophylaxis uses a three-drug regimen started promptly and discontinued if the source proves uninfected.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the case of accidental exposure, antiretroviral therapy is used as postexposure prophylaxis. A three-drug regimen has shown the most promise, especially in health care workers, and it should be discontinued if testing shows the source patient to be noninfected. Starting now and reassessing once the source's status is known is exactly the approach taken with this nurse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single agent is not used; antiretrovirals are always given in combination, and PEP is not a one-year course.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pre-exposure prophylaxis is given to at-risk people before exposure, not after a documented needlestick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prevents opportunistic infections in AIDS and does not prevent HIV acquisition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting for results forfeits the benefit of early prophylaxis, which should be started promptly after exposure.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man who is not a health care worker presents after an episode of unprotected sexual intercourse with a partner known to be HIV positive. Nonoccupational postexposure prophylaxis with antiretroviral therapy should be started within which of the following windows after the exposure?

explanation.summary: Nonoccupational postexposure prophylaxis must begin within 72 hours of exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: For people who are not health care workers, nonoccupational postexposure prophylaxis is used. It includes antiretroviral therapy within 72 hours of the exposure and should be considered for people who have had unprotected sex or a percutaneous blood exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Six hours is shorter than the stated window and would unnecessarily exclude eligible patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Seven days is beyond the window in which nPEP is given.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Twenty-four hours is earlier than the stated window of 72 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thirty days is far outside the window; by then prophylaxis would not be offered.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man who has sex with men reports inconsistent condom use with multiple partners and asks whether anything can be done to lower his chance of acquiring HIV. He has no known exposure. Which of the following is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A boosted protease inhibitor taken only during exposures

choices.label: B
